title: The Lies We Live By: Your Truth
speaker: Pastor Tito Lyro

outline.title: The Gospel of Self
subpoints: The lie that one must be enough for themselves
The danger of voluntary slavery to worldly thinking

outline.title: Identifying Three Core Lies
subpoints: The existence of subjective, individual truth
The belief that the self is sufficient to face life
The priority of the self over others

outline.title: The Nature of Truth vs. Opinion
subpoints: Distinguishing between personal opinions and objective facts
The principle: 'You can choose what you believe, but you can't change what's true'
The societal shift away from factual truth

outline.title: The Roots of Postmodernism
subpoints: Postmodernism as a reaction to modernity and the scientific method
The influence of critical theory and power dynamics

outline.title: Deconstruction and Language
subpoints: Jacques Derrida and the concept of deconstruction
The denial of authorial intent in meaning
The erosion of clear language and meaning in contemporary culture

summary:
In this second lesson of the series 'The Lies We Live By,' Pastor Tito Lyro addresses the pervasive cultural narrative that promotes the 'gospel of self.' He identifies three specific lies embedded in the modern mantra to 'live your truth': the existence of subjective truth, the sufficiency of the self, and the primacy of the self over others. The sermon argues that these ideas lead to voluntary slavery to worldly thinking and must be eliminated through biblical understanding.

The teaching distinguishes between opinion and objective truth, asserting that while individuals may choose their beliefs, they cannot alter what is factually true. This objective nature of truth is contrasted with the postmodern worldview, which is described as a reaction against modernity's reliance on logic and the scientific method. Postmodernism is characterized by a deep skepticism of absolute moral truth, viewing it instead as a construct created by groups to maintain power or function.

The sermon traces the philosophical roots of this thinking to the 1960s and the work of French philosopher Jacques Derrida, specifically his concept of 'deconstruction.' This philosophy suggests that language does not carry fixed meaning and that the listener's interpretation holds more authority than the speaker's intent. The pastor warns that this deconstruction of language leads to a muddling of meaning in society, where words are repurposed to support preconceived agendas rather than convey factual reality.
